answers.rationale: AOT artifacts must expose a C ABI; C++ mangling/ABI/STL differ across compilers. A/B/D wrong.
cudaMalloc/cudaFree are synchronous with the device and slow (us-ms). Caching allocator pools freed blocks and reuses them. A/B/D wrong or oversimplified.
AOT avoids first-call compile; standalone artifact; usually needs known shapes/dtypes. JIT compiles lazily; absorbs warmup for flexibility.
AOTInductor produces self-contained .so with generated kernels, runs from C++ without Python or Inductor at runtime.

B: C ABI entry, device pointers, no Python needed — correct. D: kernels bundled with the .so — correct. A wrong: needs a small runtime (libtorch dependency varies by version — for PyTorch 2.3~2.5 the AOTInductor artifact typically links to a small runtime not the full torch python; the strict 'full PyTorch binary distribution' claim is false in modern AOTI). C wrong: no Inductor at runtime; that's the whole point of AOT.
Standard compiler/runtime split: compiler emits kernels + fixed plan; runtime dispatches, allocates, streams, handles dynamic branches.

A: AOT eliminates JIT compile phase at cold start — correct. C: cold start = init+load+compile+warmup — correct. D: compile cache keyed by (source, shape/dtype/device, compiler-version) — correct. B wrong: caches typically produce equivalent (not bitwise-identical) outputs; small numerical differences from autotune are acceptable, not necessarily 'bugs'.

A: portable IR (PTX, SPIR-V) with driver JIT is standard — correct. B: cross compilation targets differ in ISA, GPU arch, OS ABI — correct. C: autotune on target can't be done offline without measurement infrastructure — correct. D wrong: NVCC + PTX enables cross compile for GPU.
Standard custom op contract: schema + kernels per device/dtype + autograd hook if inside autograd graph.
Dispatcher routes (op, device, dtype, layout, autograd key) to concrete kernel.

B: vendor libs often outperform compiler-generated for standard patterns due to hand-tuned tiles — correct. C: compiler can beat vendor by fusing producer/epilogue ops — correct. A wrong: no bitwise reproducibility across major library versions. D wrong: external libs don't remove need for a caching allocator.
CPU fallback = D2H copy, CPU run, H2D copy; each fallback adds a round-trip.

A: partitioning must model per-op device coverage — correct. B: subgraph partitioning with transfer ops — correct. C wrong: cross-device edges not free; partitioning must model transfer cost. D wrong: heterogeneous execution doesn't require CXL; explicit memcpy works.
IREE = MLIR-based pipeline (StableHLO/TOSA → target VM module + kernels) + HAL abstracting Vulkan/CUDA/ROCm/CPU/WebGPU.
ONNX is interchange format (standardized ops + opsets); performance depends on the runtime consuming it.

A: static shape inference helps downstream compilers with buffer planning etc — correct. C: per-op procedure defined by schema, propagates known shapes/dtypes, leaves symbolic dims when needed — correct. B/D wrong.
IR version governs file format; opset version governs operator semantics; check both fields.
opset version specifies operator schemas at that version; runtime supporting opset ≥ N must execute those ops with those semantics.
Complete package: graph + weights (with metadata) + I/O signatures + preprocessing/postprocessing/calibration + schema version tag.

A: minimize transitions — correct. B: transfer ops inserted at device boundaries — correct. D: alternating CPU/GPU in a hot loop dominates latency — correct. C wrong: cannot 'promote' CPU kernel to GPU automatically.
Kernel registry maps (op, device, dtype, layout, …) → concrete function; dispatcher uses it at run time.

B: bucketing trade-off — correct. C: symbolic shape descriptors — correct. D: shape ranges (min/opt/max) at build time; out-of-range triggers fallback/recompile — correct. A wrong: dynamic and static are not equivalent in cost.
StableHLO = versioned stable op set (MLIR dialect) as portable IR between frameworks and compilers with fwd/bwd compat.
Stream = in-order queue of device ops (same-stream in-order, cross-stream may be concurrent); event = sync marker recordable on a stream.

B: cudaStreamSynchronize(stream) blocks on that stream only — correct. C: cudaDeviceSynchronize waits all streams; overuse serializes host+device — correct. A wrong: under legacy default-stream semantics, blocking cudaMemcpy on default stream synchronizes with all streams. D wrong: overlap needs pinned host mem and correct stream setup.
Standard TensorRT flow: builder consumes network → engine (plan) with fusion, kernel selection, calibration; runtime deserializes and executes.
8 min is offline engine build cost (one-time); shouldn't be compared to per-inference eager latency; the comparison should be per-inference latency of deserialized engine.
A: optimization profiles baked in — correct. C: SM-specific plans — correct. D: no cross-major-version compat — correct. B wrong: plan doesn't need ONNX file at runtime.
Relax VM executes compiled Relax program via bytecode invoking PackedFunc kernels, allocator, device contexts, dynamic shape branches.
VM enables host-side control flow (if/while, dyn shape branches, allocator, extern function calls) around precompiled kernels; decouples control flow from native ABI.
